title: Patterns in the Closet
description: Identify familiar fabric patterns by their lines, shapes, and repeated motifs.
cardDescription: Identify familiar fabric patterns by their lines, shapes, and repeated motifs.
focus: Pattern words describe visual arrangements, while weave words describe how strands cross. A fabric can have both a particular weave and a printed pattern.
solvingTip: Look for the arrangement of colors and shapes. A plain color, crossing bands, and a teardrop motif each suggest a different word.
words: Pattern of intersecting colored bands traditionally associated with Scottish cloth
Weave producing characteristic diagonal ribs in cloth
Sturdy cotton fabric commonly made with a diagonal-rib weave
Having one uniform color rather than a repeated design
Pattern of crossing horizontal and vertical colored bands
Long narrow band in a repeated fabric design
Small square formed by intersecting contrasting lines
Small round spot in a polka-patterned fabric
Colored design applied to a fabric's surface
Arrangement produced by interlacing lengthwise and crosswise threads
Long narrow mark forming part of a striped pattern
Visual hue distinguishing one band from another

answerNotes.PAISLEY: Paisley describes a decorative motif. The cloth bearing it can be made from different fibers and weaves.
answerNotes.TARTAN: Tartan is a particular checked pattern tradition. Plaid is a broader everyday American term often used for crossing-band designs.
answerNotes.TWILL: Twill describes the interlacing structure. It is different from a pattern printed onto the surface.
answerNotes.DENIM: Denim is a fabric, commonly woven as twill. Its familiar blue appearance is not a rule for every piece of denim.
answerNotes.SOLID: Solid describes appearance here. It does not mean the cloth is stiff or physically unbendable.

title: A Button and a Zipper
description: Explore clothing fasteners through the small components that hold everyday garments together.
cardDescription: Explore clothing fasteners through the small components that hold everyday garments together.
focus: Different fasteners close in different ways. Some names identify a whole device, while others name a moving part, a single projection, or a matching opening.
solvingTip: Check singular and plural forms carefully. A whole fastener and one small component can have different answers of similar length.
words: Fastener whose interlocking rows close as a small piece slides along them
Moving part that opens or closes a zipper
One individual projection in an interlocking fastener row
Plural name for the interlocking projections of many zippers
Small loop paired with a hook in a clothing fastener
Clothing fastener whose two parts press together with a click
Small disk passed through a garment's matching opening
Curved strip or ring through which a fastening piece may pass
Bent fastening piece that catches in a matching eye
Frame and catch used to secure many belts
Small closing device joining two ends of an accessory
Waistband accessory often secured with a buckle
To join garment edges so they remain closed
Small projecting piece pulled to move a zipper's slider

answerNotes.ZIPPER: A zipper joins two rows of interlocking elements. The slider brings them together or separates them.
answerNotes.SLIDER: The slider moves along the rows. A pull tab gives the fingers something to grip while moving it.
answerNotes.TOOTH: Tooth is singular. Teeth is its irregular plural, which matters when matching the clue to the answer.
answerNotes.TEETH: Teeth is the plural form. Some zipper designs use a continuous coil rather than separate traditional teeth.
answerNotes.EYE: The eye is the receiving loop. This mechanical use differs from the body organ with the same name.

title: The Shape of a Shirt
description: Find the names for a shirt’s edges, panels, and openings through the familiar outline of a garment.
cardDescription: Find the names for a shirt’s edges, panels, and openings through the familiar outline of a garment.
focus: Some clothing terms describe where a part sits, while others describe its construction. The clues distinguish a shoulder panel, an opening reinforcement, and the finish along an edge.
solvingTip: Picture the garment from top to bottom. The location of an opening or seam can help before you know the technical term.
words: Finished strip or opening area carrying a shirt's buttons or buttonholes
Shaped garment panel across the shoulders of many shirts
Finished band or edge around the wrist end of a sleeve
Part of a shirt fitted around the neck opening
Folded and secured finish along a shirt's lower edge
Small attached compartment for carrying a pen or other item
Stitched line joining separate pieces of a shirt
Side of a shirt commonly carrying the central button opening
Shirt panel opposite the chest side
Small fastener sewn beside a shirt opening
To bend cloth over itself along a line
Lower hanging part of a shirt that may be tucked in
Plant fiber commonly used to make shirts

answerNotes.PLACKET: A placket reinforces or finishes an opening. On many shirts it runs down the center front.
answerNotes.YOKE: A yoke is a structural panel. Its name also has an unrelated farming meaning, so the garment context matters.
answerNotes.CUFF: A cuff is at the sleeve's lower end. It differs from the collar around the neck opening.
answerNotes.COLLAR: A collar frames the neck. It can have different shapes without changing the basic name.
answerNotes.HEM: A hem finishes an edge. A seam generally joins pieces together, which is a different construction role.

title: Familiar Fabric Names
description: Compare everyday fabrics through their fibers, surface textures, and methods of construction.
cardDescription: Compare everyday fabrics through their fibers, surface textures, and methods of construction.
focus: Some names identify a fiber, some a fabric, and some a weave or finish. The clues make those distinctions explicit rather than treating every textile word as the same kind of category.
solvingTip: Use a clue’s category as well as its texture description. A plant fiber and a weaving method require different answers.
words: Fabric with a dense short raised pile giving a soft surface
Smooth lustrous weave with long surface floats
Manufactured fiber made from regenerated cellulose
Textile made by matting or bonding fibers rather than ordinary weaving
Textile fiber obtained from the flax plant
Soft plant fiber from the seed hairs of its namesake crop
Animal fiber commonly shorn from sheep
Fiber produced by silkworms and used for smooth textiles
Sturdy fabric familiar from blue jeans
Rough-textured woven cloth often used for jackets
Soft napped fabric, also a word for a sheep's coat
Soft woven fabric often brushed for a fuzzy surface
Synthetic fiber familiar from stockings and lightweight fabrics
To interlace lengthwise and crosswise strands into cloth

answerNotes.VELVET: Velvet is defined by its pile construction rather than one mandatory fiber. It can be made from several materials.
answerNotes.SATIN: Satin describes a weave structure. It is not necessarily made of silk.
answerNotes.RAYON: Rayon begins with cellulose but is processed into a manufactured fiber. It differs from both unprocessed plant fiber and fully synthetic nylon.
answerNotes.FELT: Felt need not have the regular crossing threads of woven cloth. Its fibers are consolidated into a sheet.
answerNotes.LINEN: Linen comes from flax. Cotton is another plant fiber but comes from a different part of a different plant.

title: A Rainy-Day Outfit
description: Picture clothing and accessories chosen for a wet-weather walk, from a protective coat to its small closures.
cardDescription: Picture clothing and accessories chosen for a wet-weather walk, from a protective coat to its small closures.
focus: A whole garment, its body parts, and a material property have separate names. The clues describe ordinary rainwear without assuming every coat uses the same fabric or fastening.
solvingTip: Use where the item sits or what it does. A head covering, a wrist edge, and a hand-carried shelter are different objects.
words: Outer garment worn to keep rainfall off the body
Hand-held folding canopy raised against rain
Designed to prevent water from passing through under specified conditions
Attached head covering on many rain jackets
Sleeveless outer covering hanging from the shoulders
High protective footwear worn for a wet walk
Sliding front closure on many rain jackets
Small garment compartment that may have a protective flap
Outer garment worn over ordinary clothing
Flexible water-resistant material used in many rain boots
Press-together fastener used on some rainwear
Finished lower edge of a raincoat
Wrist-end finish of a rain jacket's sleeve

answerNotes.RAINCOAT: A raincoat is a garment intended for wet weather. Its materials and level of protection depend on its construction.
answerNotes.UMBRELLA: An umbrella is carried rather than worn like a coat. Its canopy and support ribs open around a central shaft.
answerNotes.WATERPROOF: Waterproof describes a material or construction property. Real products have limits depending on pressure, wear, seams, and their stated rating.
answerNotes.HOOD: A hood covers the head and is part of the garment. It differs from a separate hat or a hand-held umbrella.
answerNotes.CAPE: A cape hangs over the body without ordinary fitted sleeves. A rain cape is one wet-weather version.
